summary: Specifies how packet information is exported from a PSAMP exporting process to a collecting process. It reuses the IPFIX protocol for the transport, since the two architectures match well. This document also covers how selected packet reports are carried using IPFIX mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: Packet sampling picks out a small share of the packets passing through a router and sends those to a collector for analysis. This RFC says how to send them. It reuses IPFIX, the protocol used for traffic statistics, so a collector reads the samples with the same tools it already uses for flow records.

questions: how does psamp export packet data
what sampling methods does psamp support
subtitle: How a router sends a sample of the packets it sees to a collector, using the IPFIX protocol.

tldr.problem: Looking at every packet on a busy link is expensive and produces far too much data, so a router has to pick a subset of packets and report those.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how the sampled packets are exported with IPFIX: a Packet Report per selected packet, described by a Template Record, plus Report Interpretations that tell the collector how the packets were selected and how accurate the measurements are.
tldr.outcome: The protocol meets almost all the PSAMP requirements; the only one it does not is Export Packet compression. The RFC also says a device should not export the full payload of a conversation.

today: RFC 5476 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It is one of four documents in the PSAMP series, and it builds on the IPFIX protocol in RFC 5101 and the PSAMP information model in RFC 5477.

sections.title: Why Packet Sampling Needs Its Own Export
sections.content:
PSAMP is a contraction of the phrase Packet Sampling. The word Sampling captures the idea that only a subset of all the packets passing a network element is selected for reporting. PSAMP selection operations include random selection, deterministic selection, and deterministic approximations to random selection, which is hash-based selection.

The IP Flow Information eXport protocol (IPFIX) exports IP traffic information observed at network devices, and that matches the general protocol requirements of the PSAMP framework in RFC 5474. There are, however, architectural differences in what an export protocol has to do. The IPFIX architecture is focused on gathering and exporting IP traffic flow information, while the focus of the PSAMP framework is on exporting information on individual packets. This basic difference, and a set of derived differences in protocol requirements, are set out in section 4 of the RFC.

This document is one of a series from the PSAMP group. RFC 5474 describes the framework for network elements to select subsets of packets by statistical and other methods and to export a stream of reports on the selected packets to a collector. RFC 5475 describes the set of packet selection techniques supported by PSAMP. This document specifies the export of packet information from a PSAMP Exporting Process to a PSAMP Collecting Process, and RFC 5477 defines the information and data model for PSAMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring every packet on a busy link is too much work and produces too much data. Packet sampling picks out a small share of the packets and reports those. This RFC says how to send those reports: it reuses IPFIX, the protocol built for sending traffic statistics, so a collector can read samples with the tools it already has.

sections.title: The PSAMP Vocabulary
sections.content:
Because IPFIX is used to export the PSAMP information, the relevant IPFIX terminology is copied into this document, and the PSAMP terminology is fully consistent with the terms used in RFC 5475 and RFC 5474. Only the definitions relevant to the protocol appear here.

The Observed Packet Stream is the set of all packets observed at the Observation Point. A Packet Stream is a set of packets from the observed stream that flows past some specified point within the Metering Process; the output of the Selection Process is an example. The RFC favours the term stream over flow, because packets selected from a stream do not necessarily carry any property that distinguishes them from packets that were not selected.

The Selection Process takes the Observed Packet Stream as its input and selects a subset of it as its output. A Selector defines the action of the Selection Process on a single packet of its input; if the packet is selected it becomes an element of the output Packet Stream. Selectors may be chained, and an ordered composition of them is a Composite Selector, while a Selector that is not composite is primitive. Each primitive Selector has a unique Selector ID within the Observation Domain. The Selection Sequence is a unique value per Observation Domain describing the Observation Point and the Selector IDs through which the packets are selected.

What comes out is the Report Stream, made of two kinds of information. Packet Reports comprise a configurable subset of a packet's input to the Selection Process, including the Packet Content, information relating to its treatment such as the output interface, and its associated selection state such as a hash of the Packet Content. Report Interpretation comprises subsidiary information, relating to one or more packets, that is used for interpretation of their Packet Reports, for example the configuration parameters of the Selection Process. The Metering Process selects packets and produces the Report Stream; the Exporting Process sends that output, in the form of Export Packets, to one or more Collectors. A PSAMP Device hosts at least an Observation Point, a Selection Process and an Exporting Process, typically at a router.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names each step: the packets that pass by, the rule that picks some of them, the description of each picked packet, and the extra information that lets a collector understand those descriptions. The combination of one observation point and the ordered list of rules that picked a packet is called a selection sequence.

sections.title: How PSAMP Differs from IPFIX
sections.content:
The output of the IPFIX working group relevant to this document is structured into three documents: the IP Flow information architecture, the IPFIX protocol specifications, and the IP Flow information export information model.

From the architecture point of view, traffic flow measurement separates into two stages. In stage 1 all the processing steps act on packets: they are captured, timestamped, selected by one or more selection steps, and finally forwarded to packet classification that maps packets to flows. In stage 2 all the processing steps act on flows: after packets are classified, flows are generated or updated, flow generation and update steps may be performed repeatedly to aggregate flows, and the flows are exported. Packet sampling as described in the PSAMP framework covers only stage 1, with the packet classification replaced by Packet Report export, while IPFIX covers stage 2 as well, because it generates Flow Records out of the selected packets.

From the protocol point of view, the major difference is that the IPFIX protocol exports Flow Records while the PSAMP protocol exports Packet Reports. From a pure export point of view, IPFIX will not distinguish a Flow Record composed of several packets aggregated together from a Flow Record composed of a single packet, so the PSAMP export can be seen as a special IPFIX Flow Record containing information about a single packet. All the extensions of the IPFIX protocol that the PSAMP requirements need have already been incorporated into the IPFIX protocol, which was developed in parallel with the PSAMP protocol.

From the information model point of view the overlap between the two is quite large. Most Information Elements in the IPFIX protocol are also relevant for exporting packet information, for example all fields reporting packet header properties. Only a few, such as observedFlowTotalCount, whose value is always 1 for PSAMP, cannot be used in a meaningful way. The extensions that are required, such as the Sampling-related Information Elements, are covered by the PSAMP information model in RFC 5477.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX turns individual packets into traffic flows and reports the flows. Packet sampling stops earlier: it reports the individual packets it picked. The wire format is the same, so a sampled packet looks to a collector like a flow that happens to contain one packet.

sections.title: How IPFIX Carries PSAMP Data
sections.content:
The Template Record in the Template Set describes the different PSAMP Information Elements that will be exported to the Collector. The Collector decodes the Template Record and knows which Information Elements to expect when it receives the Data Records in the PSAMP Packet Report Data Set. Typically, in the base level of PSAMP functionality, the Template Set will contain the input sequence number, the packet fragment, which is some number of contiguous bytes from the start of the packet or from the start of the payload, and the Selection Sequence.

The Options Template Record in the Options Template Set describes the different PSAMP Information Elements that concern the Metering Process itself: the sampling and filtering functions and their associated parameters. The Collector decodes those records and knows which Information Elements to expect when it receives the Data Records in the PSAMP Report Interpretation Data Set. Typically the Options Template would contain the Selection Sequence, the sampling or filtering functions, and the parameters associated with them.

PSAMP requires all the different possibilities of the IPFIX protocol specification, that is the three types of sets (Data Set, Template Set and Options Template Set) with the two types of template records (Template Record and Options Template Record). As a consequence, PSAMP cannot rely on a subset of the IPFIX protocol specification: the entire IPFIX protocol specification MUST be implemented for the PSAMP protocol.

The RFC then checks the PSAMP requirements from the framework against the IPFIX solution. The PSAMP protocol specification meets almost all of the protocol requirements stated in the framework document, including extensibility, parallel selection processes, encrypted packets, indication of information loss, accuracy, privacy, timeliness, congestion avoidance, secure export, export rate limit and microsecond timestamp resolution. The only requirement that is not met is Export Packet compression, because the compression option mentioned in the framework document is not addressed by IPFIX.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of template are used. One tells the collector which fields each sampled packet will contain, and the other tells it how the packets were selected and with what parameters. Using IPFIX for this means a collector needs the whole IPFIX protocol, not just part of it.

sections.title: The Packet Report
sections.content:
For each Selection Sequence, and for each selected packet, a Packet Report MUST be created. Its format is specified in a Template Record contained in a Template Set. There are two types of Packet Report, the basic and the extended.

The basic Packet Report MUST contain the selectionSequenceId Information Element, which identifies the particular combination of Observation Point and Selector or Selectors used for the selection. If there is a digest function in the Selection Sequence, the report MUST also contain the hash value generated by the digest Hash Function for each selected packet, and if there is more than one digest function each hash value MUST be included in the order the functions appear in the Selection Sequence. It MUST also contain some number of contiguous bytes from the start of the packet, including the packet header and some subsequent bytes of the packet payload, or alternatively the same number of contiguous bytes starting at the beginning of the payload. The dataLinkFrameSection, mplsLabelStackSection, mplsPayloadPacketSection, ipPacketSection and ipPayloadPacketSection Information Elements are available for this use.

The Packet Report SHOULD contain a time-related Information Element that matches the accuracy of the Metering Process, typically observationTimeMicroseconds, though observationTimeSeconds, observationTimeMilliseconds and observationTimeNanoseconds are also possible. The PSAMP Device MUST be capable of exporting the number of observed packets and the number of packets selected by each instance of its Primitive Selectors, although it MAY be a configurable option not to include them; if they are exported, the Attained Selection Fraction can be calculated precisely. The contiguous Information Elements MAY be encoded with a fixed-length field or with a variable-sized field. If a fixed-length field is too long for the number of contiguous bytes in the selected packet, padding MUST NOT be used, and the Exporting Process MUST export the information either in a new Template Record with the correct fixed-length field or in a new Template Record with a variable-length field.

The extended Packet Report MAY contain other Information Elements related to the protocols used in the packet, such as source and destination IP addresses, related to the packet treatment, such as the output interface or the destination BGP autonomous system, or related to the Selection State, such as a timestamp or a hash value. It is envisaged that selecting fields for extended Packet Reports may be used to reduce reporting bandwidth, in which case the option to report some number of contiguous bytes from the start of the packet may not be exercised, and the Packet Content MAY be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: A basic packet report names the selection sequence, carries the captured bytes of the packet and a timestamp. An extended report may instead carry individual fields such as the source and destination addresses, which saves bandwidth when the collector does not need the raw packet. Each report is described by a template that the collector reads first.

sections.title: Report Interpretations
sections.content:
To make full sense of the Packet Reports, a number of additional pieces of information must be communicated to the Collector, and it is carried in four kinds of Report Interpretation, each described by an Options Template Record.

The Selection Sequence Report Interpretation gives the details of which Selectors and Observation Points are used within a Selection Sequence. It uses the selectionSequenceId as its scope field and one Information Element mapping the Observation Point selectorId as its non-scope field. The Information Element representing the Observation Point would typically be taken from the ingressInterface, egressInterface, lineCardId, exporterIPv4Address or exporterIPv6Address Information Elements, but it is not limited to those. If the packets are selected by a Composite Selector, the Selection Sequence is composed of several Primitive Selectors, and the report MUST contain the list of all the Primitive Selector IDs in the order they are used.

The Selector Report Interpretation gives the configuration details of every Selector in use. It uses the selectorId as its scope field and the selectorAlgorithm Information Element, followed by the algorithm-specific configuration parameters, as its non-scope fields.

The Selection Sequence Statistics Report Interpretation carries the Selector ID statistics. The packetsObserved Information Element contains the number of packets seen at the Observation Point, and as a consequence passed to the first Selector in the sequence, while packetsSelected contains the number of packets selected by a Selector. The Attained Selection Fraction for the sequence is the number selected by the last Selector divided by the number observed, and it can be calculated for each Selector in the same way. The statistics for the whole sequence SHOULD be taken at a single logical point in time, the input value for a Selector MUST equal the output value of the previous Selector, and the report MUST be exported periodically.

The Accuracy Report Interpretation lets the Collecting Process determine the inherent accuracy of the reported quantities, for example timestamps. It uses the Information Element the accuracy applies to as its scope, and adds a second scope with the templateId value when the accuracy is specific to a template. The accuracy SHOULD be reported with the absoluteError or the relativeError Information Element, or with both, in which case whatever is least accurate for the reported value should be used. If the accuracy of a reported quantity changes on the Metering Process, a new Accuracy Report Interpretation MUST be generated, and the Collecting Process keeps the accuracy of the latest one.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of extra message explain the samples: which rules were used and where, how each rule was configured, how many packets passed and were chosen, and how accurate the measurements are. A collector needs all four to make sense of the packets it receives.

sections.title: The Selection Methods
sections.content:
Each selection method has its own value for the selectorAlgorithm Information Element and its own configuration parameters, reported through an Options Template Record. The RFC defines the following methods.

Systematic count-based Sampling, algorithm value 1, defines the start and stop triggers for the Sampling interval by spatial packet position, that is by packet count. Its parameters are samplingPacketInterval, the number of packets selected in a row, and samplingPacketSpace, the number of packets between selections. The example in the RFC is a simple one out of ten selection, with an interval of 1 and a space of 9.

Systematic time-based Sampling, algorithm value 2, uses start and stop triggers to define the Sampling intervals. Its parameters are samplingTimeInterval and samplingTimeSpace, both in microseconds. The example is 100 microseconds out of 1000 microseconds, with an interval of 100 and a space of 900.

Random n-out-of-N Sampling, algorithm value 3, selects n elements out of the parent Population that consists of N elements. Its parameters are samplingSize, the number of packets selected, and samplingPopulation, the number of packets in the selection Population. The example is a one out of ten selection.

Uniform probabilistic Sampling, algorithm value 4, gives each element the same probability p of being selected from the parent Population. Its single parameter is samplingProbability, a floating point number. The example uses 0.15, that is 15 percent.

Property Match Filtering includes matches on fields within a packet and on properties of the router state: with this method a packet is selected if a specific field equals a predefined value. When several Information Elements are defined the filter acts as a logical AND, and the logical OR is not covered by these specifications. Because encryption alters the meaning of encrypted fields, an implementation MUST be able to recognise that the fields are not available and MUST NOT select those packets, although they must still be accounted for in the packetsObserved Information Element.

Hash-based Selection runs a Hash Function on IPv4 traffic. The fields that MUST be used as input are the IP identification field, the Flags field, the fragment offset, the source IP address, the destination IP address, and a number of bytes from the IP payload. The minimum configuration ranges are from 8 to 32 bytes and an offset from 0 to 64. Three hash functions are defined, BOB, IPSX and CRC, with selectorAlgorithm values 6, 7 and 8; only BOB is recommended, and it SHOULD be used. A hash-based Selection function MAY be configurable as a digest function, and any Selection Process configured that way MUST have the output value included in the basic Packet Report for every selected packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Several ways of choosing packets are defined. Some take every so many packets, some take packets at regular time intervals, some pick a fixed proportion at random, and some keep only packets that match a rule or whose hash falls in a chosen range. Each one has its own number, so the collector can tell which was used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As IPFIX has been selected as the PSAMP export protocol, and the PSAMP security requirements are not stricter than the IPFIX security requirements, the RFC refers to the IPFIX export protocol for the security considerations.

It adds one point of its own. In the basic Packet Report the PSAMP Device exports some number of contiguous bytes from the start of the packet, including the packet header and some subsequent bytes of the payload. The PSAMP Device SHOULD NOT export the full payload of conversations, because that would mean wiretapping, and it MUST respect local privacy laws.
sections.plainLanguage: The export protocol, IPFIX, already has its own security rules, and packet sampling does not add stricter ones. One extra rule applies to what is exported: a device should not send the whole content of a conversation, because that is wiretapping.

viz.caption: THE SELECTION METHODS, IN PLAIN TERMS

items.title: Systematic count-based
items.text: Take a fixed number of packets in a row, then skip a fixed number.

items.title: Systematic time-based
items.text: Take packets at regular time intervals, measured in microseconds.

items.title: Random n-out-of-N
items.text: Pick a set number of packets at random from a population.

items.title: Uniform probabilistic
items.text: Give every packet the same chance of being selected.

items.title: Property match filtering
items.text: Keep packets whose fields match predefined values.

items.title: Hash-based selection
items.text: Hash the packet and keep it when the result falls in a chosen range.
